title: Apply safety, health and environmental protection procedures

lessons.title: Hazards, risks and the law
lessons.html:
Safety, health and environment (SHE)

Abattoirs, grain silos and meat processing plants have many hazards: sharp knives, saws, moving conveyors, augers, live animals, slippery floors, ammonia refrigeration, dust, noise, chemicals and heavy lifting. Applying SHE procedures protects you, your team, the public and the environment.

Hazard and risk

  • A hazard is anything that can cause harm, such as a wet floor or an unguarded belt.
  • A risk is how likely it is that the hazard will cause harm, and how serious the harm would be.

Types of hazards

TypeExamples
PhysicalNoise, heat, cold rooms, moving machinery, electricity
ChemicalCleaning chemicals, ammonia, fumigants in grain stores
BiologicalZoonotic diseases from animals, blood, mould spores
ErgonomicRepetitive cutting, lifting carcass quarters or grain bags
PsychosocialFatigue, stress, long shifts

The OHS Act

The Occupational Health and Safety Act 85 of 1993 requires employers to provide and maintain, as far as reasonably practicable, a safe working environment without risk to health. Employees also have duties: to take care of their own health and safety and that of others, to follow lawful safety instructions and rules, to use protective equipment provided, and to report unsafe conditions and incidents. Health and safety representatives are appointed to help inspect the workplace and raise concerns.

Hierarchy of control

When a hazard is found, control it in this order: eliminate it, substitute it with something less dangerous, use engineering controls such as machine guards, use administrative controls such as procedures and training, and finally use personal protective equipment (PPE). PPE is the last line of defence, not the first.

lessons.title: Safe work procedures and emergencies
lessons.html:
Working safely every day

Personal protective equipment

  • Steel-toe or safety gumboots with non-slip soles
  • Cut-resistant gloves and chain-mail aprons for knife work, where required
  • Hearing protection in noisy areas
  • Dust masks or respirators in grain handling where dust is present
  • Goggles, chemical gloves and aprons when handling chemicals
  • Warm clothing for cold rooms and freezers

Inspect PPE before use. Report damaged PPE and do not use it.

Machine safety and lockout

Before cleaning, unblocking or repairing a machine such as a conveyor, saw, mincer or auger, it must be isolated and locked out. Switch off, isolate the power, fit your personal lock and tag, and test that it cannot start. Never remove guards while a machine is running. Never reach into a moving machine.

Confined spaces and grain

Silos, bins and tanks are confined spaces. They can contain toxic gases or too little oxygen, and flowing grain can bury a person within seconds. Never enter a silo or bin unless you are trained, have a permit, the space has been tested, and a standby person is present. Grain dust can also explode, so control ignition sources and keep areas clean.

Emergencies

  • Know where the emergency exits, assembly point, fire extinguishers and first aid boxes are.
  • Know the alarm signal and evacuation procedure.
  • If you smell ammonia, leave the area immediately upwind and raise the alarm. Do not try to stop a leak unless trained and equipped.
  • Report every incident and near miss, no matter how small.

Manual handling

Bend your knees, keep the back straight, hold the load close and avoid twisting. Use trolleys, rails and hoists where available, and get help for heavy loads.

lessons.title: Protecting health and the environment
lessons.html:
Health at work

Some harm develops slowly. Noise causes permanent hearing loss over years. Repetitive knife work can cause wrist and shoulder injuries. Dust can damage lungs. Zoonotic diseases such as brucellosis can pass from animals to people through contact with blood and fluids. Protect your health by using PPE, taking part in medical surveillance programmes, washing hands, covering cuts and reporting symptoms to your supervisor or clinic.

Housekeeping

Good housekeeping prevents many accidents. Clean spills immediately, keep walkways clear, put tools and hoses away, and remove waste regularly. A tidy plant is a safer plant.

Environmental protection

Meat and grain operations can harm the environment if waste is not controlled:

  • Effluent: blood and wash water are high in organic matter. They must go through the plant's effluent system and must not be released into rivers or the veld. The National Water Act 36 of 1998 protects water resources.
  • Solid waste: condemned material, manure, paunch contents and packaging must be handled according to plant procedures and applicable regulations.
  • Chemicals: store in bunded areas, use the correct amounts, never pour down storm water drains.
  • Air: control dust from grain intake and odours from rendering and waste areas.
  • Water and energy: close taps, fix leaks, switch off equipment that is not needed.

Spills

If a chemical or fuel spill happens: warn others, stop the source if it is safe, contain it with spill kit absorbents, report it and follow the clean-up procedure. Do not wash it into drains.

Reporting

Report hazards, incidents, near misses and environmental spills to your supervisor or SHE representative. Reports help the company prevent the next incident; they are not about blame.

Key points

  • A hazard can cause harm; risk is how likely and how serious the harm is.
  • Under the OHS Act, employers and employees both have safety duties.
  • Use the hierarchy of control; PPE is the last line of defence.
  • Lock out machines before cleaning or repairs; never enter silos without a permit and standby person.
  • Keep effluent, chemicals and waste out of rivers and storm water drains.
  • Report all incidents, near misses and spills.
